explanations.answer: They don't wash their hands before they eat
explanations.explanation: Hands, friend. The Pharisees and scribes, religious leaders who came from Jerusalem, say, “They do not wash their hands before they eat.” That's the whole charge. They call it breaking the tradition of the elders, which is a big name for a very small sink moment.

explanations.answer: They don't fast twice a week like others
explanations.explanation: I can see why this one looked believable, but fasting isn't what they bring up. The Pharisees and scribes, religious leaders from Jerusalem, say the disciples break the tradition of the elders because “They do not wash their hands before they eat.” So the charge is about hands, plain and simple. Nobody mentions a fasting schedule here.

explanations.answer: They don't pray three times every day
explanations.explanation: Prayer schedules never come up in this charge. The Pharisees and scribes, religious leaders who came from Jerusalem, say, “They do not wash their hands before they eat.” That's the tradition of the elders they say the disciples break. It's all about hands, baker, so keep your eyes on the sink.

explanations.answer: Why they break God's command for their tradition
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus replies, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?” They asked about the elders' tradition, and He asks about God's command. Same question shape, but now it's pointed the other way, and I think that landed in the room like a dropped tray.

explanations.answer: Why they came all this way to ask about hands
explanations.explanation: Jesus never questions their trip. He replies, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?” So He doesn't ask about the miles or the hands. He goes straight to God's command and their tradition.

explanations.answer: Why they never wash their own hands either
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't throw their own hands back at them. The text has Him reply, “And why do you break the command of God for the sake of your tradition?” He's talking about God's command, not their soap habits. That's a much bigger question than a sink.

True. Jesus says, “For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’…” That's the first command He points to. Then He adds a second one right behind it, about anyone who curses his father or mother. He's reaching for God's words, not the elders' words.

This one is actually true. Jesus says, “For God said, ‘Honor your father and mother’…” That's the first command He points to. The second comes right after it, about anyone who curses his father or mother, so the honor command goes first.

It goes the other way, friend. In their teaching, once he says it's a gift devoted to God, “he need not honor his father or mother with it.” So he's let off, not held to it. That's why Jesus says they nullify the word of God for the sake of their tradition.

Right. Their teaching says that once he says it's a gift devoted to God, “he need not honor his father or mother with it.” So he doesn't have to honor them with it. Jesus says this is how they nullify the word of God for the sake of their tradition, because God's command said to honor your father and mother.

Far, far away. The words say, “These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.” The lips are in the room and the heart is out the door. Jesus says Isaiah, Israel's prophet, prophesied correctly about them.

It's the opposite. The words from Isaiah, Israel's prophet, say, “These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.” The lips are close, but the hearts are not. That gap is exactly what Jesus is pointing at.

That would be a lovely picture, but it isn't this one. The words say, “These people honor Me with their lips, but their hearts are far from Me.” So the hearts are far from Him, not fixed on Him. Isaiah, Israel's prophet, is who Jesus says spoke these words.

Men is the one. The words say, “They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.” So the rules they're teaching come from people. That's the thread running through this whole conversation.
Angels aren't in this line at all. The words say, “They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.” The rules come from men. Nobody in the heavenly choir gets the blame here.
No kings in this line, baker. The words say, “They worship Me in vain; they teach as doctrine the precepts of men.” The word is men, plain and simple. Nobody in a crown is mentioned.

explanations.answer: What comes out of his mouth
explanations.explanation: That's the one. Jesus tells the crowd, “A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.” I sample every batch I bake, so this was a relief to hear. The focus moves from the plate to what comes out.
That's exactly the reverse of what Jesus says. He tells the crowd, “A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.” So what goes in isn't the issue. What comes out is.

Hands are where the Pharisees started, but Jesus doesn't say this to the crowd. He says, “A man is not defiled by what enters his mouth, but by what comes out of it.” So it's about what comes out of the mouth. We'll see Him come back around to hands at the end.

Offended is right. The disciples tell Jesus, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?” I think the disciples were a little nervous bringing it up. That's the kind of news you deliver quietly.

Nobody's clapping in this scene. The disciples tell Jesus, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?” So the Pharisees were offended, not amazed. The text gives us that word.

Confused is close to a feeling you might expect, but it isn't the one the text gives. The disciples say, “Are You aware that the Pharisees were offended when they heard this?” So the word is offended. Remember that, baker.
True. Jesus says, “If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.” Notice it's both of them, not just the follower. He says this right after calling the Pharisees blind guides.

It's actually true. Jesus says, “If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit.” Both of them go down, the leader and the one following. He's talking about the Pharisees, whom He calls blind guides.

Yes. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asks Him to explain the parable. Jesus asks first, “Do you still not understand?” Peter asked for help and got a question before the answer. I know that feeling too.

explanations.answer: Why they told Him about the Pharisees
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't ask them that. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asks Him to explain the parable, and Jesus asks, “Do you still not understand?” The question is about whether they understand. The Pharisees aren't the topic of it.

explanations.answer: If the crowd had understood it
explanations.explanation: The crowd isn't the one in question here. Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, asks for the explanation, and Jesus asks the disciples, “Do you still not understand?” So the question is about them. Then He explains.

explanations.answer: Into the stomach and then out
explanations.explanation: That's the route. Jesus says, “…whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?” So food takes a trip through and out. It doesn't reach the heart, and that's His whole point.

explanations.answer: Into the blood and stays there
explanations.explanation: That's not the trip Jesus describes. He says, “…whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?” So it doesn't stay. It goes through and out.

explanations.answer: Into the mind and changes it
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't send it to the mind. He says, “…whatever enters the mouth goes into the stomach and then is eliminated?” It goes to the stomach and then out. So what goes into the mouth doesn't change a man the way what comes out of the heart does.

Heart. Jesus says, “But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man.” The mouth is just the doorway, and the heart is where it starts. That connects right back to the Isaiah words about hearts far from God.
Lungs supply the air, but that's not what Jesus names. He says, “But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man.” So the source is the heart.
The throat is only on the way out. Jesus says, “But the things that come out of the mouth come from the heart, and these things defile a man.” The source is the heart, not the throat.

Both are on His list. Jesus says, “…evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.” This is a heavy list, and I think it's meant to make us look inward. Jesus says these come out of the heart.
Neither of those is on His list. Jesus says, “…evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.” It's a heavy list. Jesus says these come out of the heart.

Worry and fear aren't named in this list. Jesus says, “…evil thoughts, murder, adultery, sexual immorality, theft, false testimony, and slander.” That's a heavy list to read. Jesus says these come out of the heart.

It's the reverse, friend. Jesus ends with, “These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him.” So the very thing the Pharisees and scribes started with doesn't defile. The conversation comes full circle, and the answer is no.

False is right. Jesus says, “These are what defile a man, but eating with unwashed hands does not defile him.” It's the same hands the Pharisees and scribes started with. He's come all the way back to the first question and answered it.
